passages.t: The white horse and the red
passages.happening:
The Lamb who took the scroll in chapter 5 now begins to break its seals. “Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say in a thunderous voice” (verse 1). The voice calls, “Come!”

John sees a rider: “So I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer” (verse 2).

The Lamb opens the second seal, and the second living creature says, “Come!” Another rider goes out: “It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Four horsemen ride out in the first four seals, and they belong together. Each time the Lamb opens a seal. Each time a living creature calls, “Come!” And each rider is given something: a crown, permission, a sword, authority. That small word, given, matters. None of these powers acts on its own. Each is allowed, and each has a limit.

What comes out of the scroll first is not the end of the world. It is the kind of world the churches already lived in. The first hearers knew these riders from experience. Beyond the river Euphrates lay the Parthian empire, Rome's great rival in the east, famous for its archers on horseback. It had beaten Roman armies in 53 BC and again in AD 62. A crowned rider with a bow may well have made readers in Asia think of that threat.

The red horse takes ‘peace from the earth’. Rome's proudest boast was the Pax Romana, the Roman peace. The civil wars of AD 68 and 69, when four emperors ruled in a single year, showed how easily that peace could be lost. The red rider's ‘great sword’ is the sword of war, and of people killing one another.

The whole series follows closely what Jesus taught his disciples on the Mount of Olives: wars, nations rising against nations, famines, earthquakes, the persecution of believers, and then signs in the sun, moon and stars. And Jesus said of those things, ‘These are the beginning of birth pains’.
passages.ot: The coloured horses come from Zechariah's visions, where horses patrol the earth for the LORD: “I looked out into the night and saw a man riding on a red horse” with “red, sorrel, and white horses” behind him (Zechariah 1:8), and later chariots drawn by red, black, white and dappled horses (Zechariah 6:2-3).
passages.hard:
What do the seals describe, and when?

Christians read the seals, like the rest of chapters 4 to 22, in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists read them as troubles that came on the first readers' world: war, famine and death in the first century, leading to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or to God's judgment on persecuting Rome. Historicists read the seals, trumpets and bowls as a series of events in the church's history, one after another, from John's day to the end. Futurists read them as events still to come, in a time of great trouble just before Christ returns. Idealists read them as pictures of what happens in every age: conquest, war, scarcity and death are always loose in the world until Christ comes.

Readers also differ on whether the seals, trumpets and bowls follow one another in time, or tell the same story more than once from different angles. That second idea goes back to Victorinus of Pettau, who died about 304 and wrote the oldest Latin commentary on Revelation that survives.

What these notes will not do is tie any rider to a nation, a leader, a war or an event of our own day. Such matches have been made in every generation, and every one has passed. Jesus' own words about wars stand over this chapter: “When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come” (Mark 13:7).
passages.asks: Ask how it helps you, or troubles you, to think of the evils of history as permitted but limited. Ask what you are tempted to read into the news that the Bible does not say. And ask what it would mean to hear Jesus' words, ‘do not be alarmed’, in a world of war.

passages.t: The black horse and the pale
passages.happening:
The Lamb opens the third seal, and the third living creature says, “Come!” John writes, “Then I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales” (verse 5). John hears a voice from among the living creatures: “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine” (verse 6).

The Lamb opens the fourth seal, and the fourth living creature says, “Come!” John writes, “Then I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The black horse brings famine, or at least terrible prices. A denarius was about a labourer's wage for a day. A quart of wheat was about one person's food for a day. So a day's work buys bread for one, and nothing for a family. Barley was the cheaper grain of the poor. Why oil and wine are spared is not certain. Some point out that grain fails in a drought more quickly than olive trees and vines with deep roots. Others link the line with an order of the emperor Domitian, about AD 92, reported by Suetonius, to cut back vineyards in the provinces, an order later withdrawn.

The last horse is ‘pale green’. The Greek word, chlōros, is the greenish pale of a corpse. Its rider is named: Death. And Hades follows him. Hades is the Greek name for the place of the dead, used in the New Testament for the Hebrew Sheol.

They are given authority over ‘a fourth of the earth’. That is a real and terrible share, but it is a share. Death is limited. And remember who holds the keys. In the first chapter the risen Christ said, ‘I hold the keys of Death and of Hades’ (1:18). Death rides out only when the Lamb opens the seal, and it does not have the last word.
passages.ot:
The four ways of death in verse 8 are Ezekiel's four judgments: “sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague” (Ezekiel 14:21).

And the black and pale horses join the coloured horses of Zechariah's vision: “The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses” (Zechariah 6:2).
passages.hard:
Does this mean that famines, plagues and disasters today are God punishing the people they strike?

No. The picture shows that the evils of this world are not outside God's rule, and that they are limited. It does not tell anyone why a particular person suffers. Jesus refused to read disasters that way. Of eighteen people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No” (Luke 13:4-5). And nothing here makes anyone's illness or death a sign of God's judgment. When his disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

So these verses must never be used to say that a person, a town or a people struck by famine, illness or disaster is being punished for their sins. And they give no one a timetable. The riders have been loose in every age; Jesus called such things ‘the beginning of birth pains’, not the end (Mark 13:8).
passages.asks: Ask what it means for the poor that a day's wage buys only a day's bread, and who in your own town lives like that. Ask what difference it makes that Christ holds the keys of Death. And ask whether you have ever heard a disaster explained as God's punishment, and how this passage, and Jesus' words, answer it.

passages.happening:
The Lamb opens the fifth seal, and the scene moves from earth to heaven: “I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld” (verse 9).

John hears them cry out: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?” (verse 10).

“Then each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer, until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
These are people who were killed because they would not let go of God's word and their witness to Jesus. The Greek word for testimony, marturia, is the word from which the English ‘martyr’ comes, because in the early church witness so often cost a life. In Pergamum, Antipas had already been killed (2:13).

They are ‘under the altar’. In the tabernacle, the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar. Their lives were poured out in the same way. God has not forgotten them. They are close to him.

Their cry is ‘How long?’ It is the cry of the psalms of lament. Scripture keeps it as a faithful prayer, not as a sin to be edited out. Every suffering believer who has asked ‘How long?’ is in good company here.

And they are answered. Each is given a white robe, the sign of being made clean and of being proved right. They are told to rest. And they are told that God knows the number of those who will suffer as they did. Their suffering is seen, it is counted, and it has an end.

The passage honours those who were killed for their faith. It does not make death something to seek. They did not choose to die. They were killed by others, because they would not deny Christ. What they receive is rest, a robe and a promise.
passages.ot:
Pouring out blood at the base of the altar is the law of sacrifice: “he is to pour out the rest of the bull’s blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering” (Leviticus 4:7).

The cry is the psalm's: “How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?” (Psalm 79:5). And the angel in Zechariah asked the same of God: “How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 1:12).
passages.hard:
The martyrs ask God to avenge their blood. Isn't that at odds with Jesus' command to love enemies?

It can sound like a prayer for revenge, and readers are right to notice it. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did the same as he died (Acts 7:60).

Several things are worth weighing. The martyrs do not take vengeance; they hand it to God, which is what the New Testament asks of believers: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19). The word they use, ekdikeō, means to give justice to someone who has been wronged. Their request is for justice to be done in the open, for God to show that the world's verdict on them was false. A God who never judged would leave murderers in the right and victims forgotten. And many interpreters note that Revelation keeps the door of repentance open even in judgment (9:20-21; 11:13; 14:6-7). Readers differ on how to hold love of enemies and longing for justice together. The Bible holds both, and so do these martyrs, who are told to rest and wait rather than to strike.

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have ever prayed ‘How long?’, and what you needed from God when you did. Ask what it means that God gives the suffering a robe and rest before he gives them answers. And ask how you can stand with Christians who suffer for their faith today.

passages.t: The great day of their wrath
passages.happening:
The Lamb opens the sixth seal, and John sees the whole world shaken: “there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind” (verses 12-13). “The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place” (verse 14).

He sees people of every rank hide: “Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free man hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains” (verse 15).

And he hears what they say: “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
The fifth seal asked ‘How long?’ The sixth gives a glimpse of the answer: a day when every human power stands before God.

The pictures are the prophets' pictures of ‘the day of the LORD’: a dark sun, a red moon, falling stars, a sky rolled up like a scroll. The first hearers knew earthquakes well. Tacitus records one in AD 17 that ruined twelve cities, among them Sardis and Philadelphia, and another that destroyed Laodicea around AD 60. Here the shaking reaches the whole created order.

Notice the list in verse 15. It moves down the social order, from kings to nobles, commanders, the rich and the mighty, to slaves and free people. No rank escapes. The powerful who ruled the earth now hide in caves.

And notice the startling phrase: ‘the wrath of the Lamb’. The Greek word for wrath, orgē, in Scripture is not a loss of temper. It is God's settled, just opposition to evil. The one who died for sinners is not indifferent to evil. The Lamb who was slain is also the judge.

The chapter ends on a question: ‘who is able to withstand it?’ Chapter 7 answers it before the seventh seal is opened.
passages.ot:
The darkened sun and blood-red moon are Joel's: “The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Joel 2:31).

The rolled-up sky is Isaiah's: “The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree” (Isaiah 34:4). So are the people in hiding: “Men will flee to caves in the rocks and holes in the ground, away from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty” (Isaiah 2:19).

And the cry to the mountains is Hosea's: “Then they will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us!’ and to the hills, ‘Fall on us!’” (Hosea 10:8). Jesus used the same words on the road to the cross (Luke 23:30).
passages.hard:
Is this the end of the world? And should this passage make me afraid?

Christians read the sixth seal in the four ways the book page sets out, as they read the other seals (see the note on verses 1-4), and these notes do not choose. On every reading it is a glimpse of the day of reckoning, when every human power stands before God. These notes set no date for it. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36).

The picture is meant to be sober, not to be enjoyed. It is spoken to churches that were being crushed, to tell them that the powerful will not escape justice. It is not a threat aimed at frightened believers. And the question it ends with, ‘who is able to withstand it?’, is answered at once in the next chapter, by people sealed and kept by God, and a multitude in white robes before the Lamb.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what people hide behind today when they feel exposed before God: wealth, rank, busyness, distraction. Ask what it means that the judge is the Lamb who was slain for sinners. And ask who you would trust to stand for you on that day.
